faq.question: What is Champollion?
faq.answer: Champollion is machine translation development and deployment on rails with guardrails. In plain words: a family, a school or a community can build a translator for its own language from the sentences it already has, on its own computer. An AI assistant can walk you through every step, in order (the rails), while checks stop the usual mistakes and keep your words under the control of the people who hold them (the guardrails). It doesn't promise your translator will be good; it promises you'll always know how close its translations come to the way a speaker would say them (What this is: /docs/what-is-champollion; How it works: /docs/how-it-works). It was built with low-resource and Indigenous language communities in mind. To begin, read Before you begin (/docs/before-you-begin), then Start a project (/docs/start). {{UNRELEASED:The step-by-step tools come with the next version.}} There are other doors too: Getting help (/docs/getting-help), Join a project (/docs/join-a-project), Translate an app or website (/docs/translate-an-app-or-website), and Host a sealed test (/docs/host-a-sealed-test).

faq.question: Is Champollion free? Is it open source? Does it cost anything?
faq.answer: The tools are free for families, schools, charities, public services like hospitals, governments' own offices, and personal or research projects. Commercial use (a language app, a paid service) isn't covered by the free licence, but if your speaker community wants to use the tools commercially, ask, and the licence is free (Who may use it, and what it costs: /docs/getting-started/who-may-use-this). The licences themselves: the project tool (champollion), the MCP server and nmt-forge are under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0, which is not an open-source licence; the evaluation harness (mt-eval-harness) is open source under AGPL-3.0-or-later. Champollion takes no share of anything a community earns from its own language. You need a computer, and an AI assistant, or any outside model service you choose, may have its own cost. Help is optional: "Having trouble, or want help with your project? Let's talk." There's no price list, and you never need us to finish (Getting help: /docs/getting-help).

faq.question: What is the champollion CLI and what does it do?
faq.answer: `champollion` is the project tool: a command you run on your own computer. It has two jobs. One is translating an app's or website's own text, which is one of Champollion's doors, Translate an app or website (/docs/translate-an-app-or-website): `npx champollion sync` finds your language files, translates only what's missing or changed, checks every translation before writing it, and leaves the rest alone. The checks catch broken output (an empty answer, the original copied back, words repeating in a loop, the wrong alphabet), not wrong meaning, so a speaker still has the last word. The full reference, with watch, lint, verify, audit and XLIFF export, is App and site translation (/docs/intro). Its other job is walking a language project on the rails: `champollion new` starts one, and `champollion next` always names the next step (Start a project: /docs/start). {{UNRELEASED:The step-by-step tools come with the next version.}} It's free for noncommercial use (Who may use it, and what it costs: /docs/getting-started/who-may-use-this).

faq.question: How do I install and run the CLI?
faq.answer: It depends what you want to do. To translate an app's or website's text (Translate an app or website: /docs/translate-an-app-or-website), you need Node.js 20.11 or newer. Run `npx champollion sync` with no install, or add it with `npm install --save-dev champollion` (Installation: /docs/getting-started/installation). Set one provider key (OpenRouter is recommended; Gemini has a free tier), or point it at a model on your own machine, which needs no key. The Quick Start (/docs/getting-started/quick-start) walks you through your first file. To build a translator for your language on the rails, install the project tool with `npm install -g champollion`, start a project with `champollion new`, and ask `champollion next` for the next step (Start a project: /docs/start). {{UNRELEASED:The step-by-step tools come with the next version; until then, Before you begin (/docs/before-you-begin) is what you can do today.}}

faq.question: What translation methods does the CLI support?
faq.answer: For translating an app's or website's text, you choose a method for each language pair, and you can mix them in one project (Translation Methods: /docs/guides/translation-methods). The choices: `llm` (any model through OpenRouter; the default), `llm-coached` (the same, plus grammar rules, a dictionary and style notes), the direct `openai`, `anthropic` and `gemini` methods, `local` (a model on your own machine or server, including one you trained with nmt-forge, so text never leaves your infrastructure), the translation services `google-translate`, `deepl`, `microsoft-translator`, `libretranslate`, `tilde` and `translated`, `api` (an HTTP endpoint you host), and installed method plugins. A pair can also name a fallback method. A method that calls a company's service sends your app's words to that company, so use those for text that's fine to share (Translate an app or website: /docs/translate-an-app-or-website).

faq.question: What is the Network and the leaderboard?
faq.answer: The Network is the shared, public side of measuring translators: the leaderboard, and the map drawn from it. The leaderboard is a public record of scored translation runs (Leaderboard and publishing: /docs/reference/leaderboard). Anyone can add to it: you run the evaluation harness, `mt-eval`, on your own machine against a registered dataset, and publish the result as a run card. The board keeps the card; it doesn't run your method for you. The network map shows which language pairs have been measured, and which haven't. A place on the board says how one method scored on one dataset under one metric. It doesn't say the translations are good, and it gives nobody permission to use a method on a community's language. There are two kinds of benchmark: public ones on open datasets, and sealed ones a host keeps on their own machine, where entrants never see the sentences and only scores come out (Host a sealed test: /docs/host-a-sealed-test). Building your own translator doesn't need the board: scores can be shared without the sentences, and only if you choose to (Your words, your rules: /docs/your-words-your-rules). The board itself is at /leaderboard.

faq.question: Is the leaderboard populated yet? What can I actually trust on it?
faq.answer: The leaderboard is live, public and open for submissions. Its contents change, so the docs don't describe them: read the board itself at /leaderboard (Leaderboard and publishing: /docs/reference/leaderboard). What you can trust: every row today is self-benchmarked, meaning the person who ran it published it. Champollion Verified would mean the score was re-derived from the submitted outputs against the pinned references, but that check is a maintainer command run by hand, so no row is promoted on arrival (Submission Rules: /docs/network/leaderboard/rules). No community speaker review has been done, so no score on the site is a quality verdict, and no prize is open. A score describes a method on one dataset under one metric, not the next sentence it will translate. Technical limits (/docs/network/honest-limitations) lists everything that is not claimed.

faq.question: How do I submit a benchmark run or a method to the leaderboard?
faq.answer: Install the evaluation harness with `python3 -m pip install mt-eval-harness` (it gives you the `mt-eval` command), run your method against a registered dataset with `mt-eval run`, naming the model by its exact slug (short aliases are refused), and review the run card it writes. Preview with `mt-eval publish <report> --dry-run`, then publish to the live board with `mt-eval publish <report> --prod`. The full walkthrough is Submit a Method (/docs/network/getting-started/submit-a-method). Every row arrives self-benchmarked. Champollion Verified re-scoring is a maintainer command run by hand, so today rows stay self-benchmarked (Submission Rules: /docs/network/leaderboard/rules). A web upload and a submission API are planned but not live, and there's no pull-request intake: `mt-eval publish` is the working path. And never train on the evaluation data: that gets a method disqualified.

faq.question: How is a method scored? What do the scores mean?
faq.answer: Every run is scored the way the field scores translation (scoring standard/1). The headline is corpus-level chrF++: a score out of 100 for how closely the translations' letters and words match the reference translations, given with its 95% confidence interval, a range showing how sure the measurement is. BLEU, spBLEU, TER and, when it was computed, COMET are reported beside it, never blended in; diagnostics such as exact match and FST (word-form) acceptance are reported separately. The old weighted composite and its quality tiers are retired. Whether one translator is better than another is decided by a paired significance test on chrF++, not by comparing two numbers. On the rails, the same test judges each round on your practice sentences; with fewer than 50 practice sentences, the tools don't call it, and the speaker's marks decide (The guardrails: /docs/guardrails). These are automated measures of closeness, not a promise of quality: a fluent speaker decides what is fit to use. Reading the numbers (/docs/reading-the-numbers) explains each number in plain words; the Scoring Specification (/docs/network/specifications/scoring) is the full rule.

faq.question: What is 'the one rule' about training data?
faq.answer: Never train on the evaluation data. A method exposed to a benchmark set, as training data, few-shot examples, dictionary entries or prompt material, is disqualified (Leaderboard and publishing: /docs/reference/leaderboard; Submission Rules: /docs/network/leaderboard/rules). Train on separate data, and keep the test set out of it. Registered evaluation datasets are marked do-not-train for exactly this reason. The rails apply the same rule to your own project: the test sentences a speaker checked are set aside before any teaching starts and never learned from, and copies and near-copies of them are taken out of what the translator learns from (The guardrails: /docs/guardrails).

faq.question: Can I really help if I'm not a programmer?
faq.answer: Yes. The most important part of building a translator needs no computer at all (Before you begin: /docs/before-you-begin): talking with your speakers, agreeing how to spell, deciding who your words belong to, and writing sentences down. One person says a sentence in the language; another types it into a spreadsheet with its English beside it. A speaker's most valuable work is checking the translator's drafts: Y if it's right, N if it's wrong (then write how you would say it), ? if you're not sure (Working with speakers: /docs/working-with-speakers). For the steps that do use a computer, an AI assistant can do the typing while you answer the questions that are yours. You can also offer sentences or a word list to a project someone else is running, once projects are listed on Join a project (/docs/join-a-project). Paying speakers for their time is right, and in a project it's for the people leading it to decide.

faq.question: I'm a language community or speaker — how do I get involved, and can I own my test set?
faq.answer: Start with Before you begin (/docs/before-you-begin): talk with your speakers, agree how to spell, decide who your words belong to, and start writing sentences down. Then Start a project (/docs/start), with an AI assistant or on your own; the tools run on your own computer. {{UNRELEASED:The step-by-step tools come with the next version; until then, Before you begin is what you can do today.}} Yes, your test sentences are yours: a speaker checks them, they stay on your computer, and no translator ever learns from them (Set aside your test sentences: /docs/your-test-sentences). The people who hold the words decide what happens to them and to anything built from them (Your words, your rules: /docs/your-words-your-rules). If you'd like others to try their translators on your sentences without ever seeing them, see Host a sealed test (/docs/host-a-sealed-test). "Having trouble, or want help with your project? Let's talk." Write to info@champollion.dev.

faq.question: I'm an ML researcher — how do I get involved?
faq.answer: Build a method and measure it. Install the harness (`python3 -m pip install mt-eval-harness`, which gives you `mt-eval`), score your method against registered datasets, and publish run cards (Submit a Method: /docs/network/getting-started/submit-a-method). A method can be a coached LLM, an FST-gated pipeline, a fine-tuned model, a dictionary lookup, or people: Methods and gates (/docs/agents/methods) shows the recipes, and the Method Interface (/docs/network/specifications/methods) defines the protocol. Scores are corpus chrF++ with a 95% interval, and "better" is a paired significance test (Scoring Specification: /docs/network/specifications/scoring). You can also run open items off the public queue with your own key (Contributing Compute: /docs/network/getting-started/contributing-compute). Working on an Indigenous language? Build a relationship with the community before you start, and develop on openly licensed data (Ownership & Terms: /docs/network/sovereignty/ownership-transfer).

faq.question: I'm a professional translator or a translation vendor — is there a place for me here?
faq.answer: Yes. A human translation service (a community office, an agency or an individual translator) can be proposed for listing through Submit to the Index (/docs/network/getting-started/submit-to-the-index). A maintainer reviews every submission by hand, and your contact details go to the maintainer out-of-band, never into the public issue. People's own translations can also be scored like any other method: a `human` method, scored with `mt-eval test` (Methods and gates: /docs/agents/methods). And for app and site translation, the XLIFF workflow lets a project export machine drafts for professional review in tools such as memoQ, Trados, Phrase or OmegaT, and import your corrections back (Working with Professional Translators: /docs/guides/professional-translators).

faq.question: What does 'sovereignty-aspirant' mean?
faq.answer: It means we build so that communities can own and control their language data, and anything made from it, without claiming we've got there. Whether we succeed is for communities to judge (Your words, your rules: /docs/your-words-your-rules). As The Atlas (/docs/atlas) puts it, the project is sovereignty-aspirant, not sovereignty-certified: we build the mechanisms and describe them honestly, and whether they honour community ownership and control of language data is for the communities involved to determine, not us. The project is not validated, certified or approved against any Indigenous data-sovereignty framework; no assessment has taken place, and none is implied (What data sovereignty means when you write it into software: /docs/learn/data-sovereignty). If you think we fall short, tell us: that's what the objections channel is for.

faq.question: What is data sovereignty here — do you store or scrape my language data?
faq.answer: No. By default your files stay on your computer: the tools bring them in where they are and show your AI assistant only counts and column names. The rule is simple: the people who hold the words decide what happens to them, and the tools write those decisions down and obey them (Your words, your rules: /docs/your-words-your-rules). Each file gets a note saying who it belongs to, whether the speakers agreed, whether a translator may learn from it, and whether it may ever leave the computer, and every tool obeys it. Champollion doesn't host collections: the tools point to where a collection is published and fetch it from there. The two exceptions are files someone offers through Join a project (kept on Champollion's project storage) and a published score for an openly licensed test set, which can include its sentences. Some things no tool can stop: an AI assistant that runs on a company's computers can open your files if you ask it to, so for words you want kept private, use an assistant that runs on your own computer, or don't ask it to open them. Where your data goes (/your-data) shows every case side by side.

faq.question: What are the licensing lanes, and how do they work?
faq.answer: When you register an evaluation corpus, you make two separate choices (Registering Corpora & Exposure Lanes: /docs/network/sovereignty/registering-corpora). The first is what leaves your machine: local-only (the default: nothing), registered privately (a description only), registered publicly (a description plus a pointer to where it's published), or sealed (a content-free description; the locked set stays with you). The text itself is never uploaded in any of them. The second is the licence lane, what the corpus may be used for: public (it may rank on the public board), non-commercial research-only (it can be benchmarked, but it's kept out of every commercial, prize and API path), or private (your own scored runs; the reference sentences are never published). Enforcement is mechanical: the commercial lane is strict, the research lane is lenient, and quarantine always wins, so an improper subset can never rank in any lane. A corpus under a modified, bespoke or unstated licence also refuses remote model-API evaluation until its rights-holder's consent is recorded (Submission Rules: /docs/network/leaderboard/rules).

faq.question: Can my community keep its test set secret and still have methods scored against it?
faq.answer: Yes. That's a sealed test (Host a sealed test: /docs/host-a-sealed-test). Your test sentences are locked with a key, on your computer. People send in their translators, your computer runs each one on the locked sentences, and only the scores come out, never the sentences and never the translations. You set the terms before anyone competes: what counts as good enough, what happens to a winning method, and whether there's a prize at all. The tools for this work today, but it isn't on the rails yet: it means following a longer manual, Run a Sovereign Contest (/docs/network/sovereignty/run-a-sovereign-contest). On keys: they're organizer-held today, held by whoever locks the set; community key custodians: none appointed yet; Champollion holds no key shares (Technical limits: /docs/network/honest-limitations).

faq.question: Do speakers get paid, and how much?
faq.answer: In your own project, paying speakers for their time is right, and it's for the people leading the project to decide (Working with speakers: /docs/working-with-speakers). Credit people the way they want: by name, by family, by community, or not at all. Champollion takes no share of anything a community earns, and anything a sponsor gives passes straight through. For Champollion's own planned speaker check of its scores, the Speaker Validation Protocol (/docs/network/specifications/speaker-validation) publishes a rate of $50–65 CAD per hour of a bilingual speaker's rating time, paid whether or not the ratings are used. That work isn't funded yet, so it hasn't started, and no one is asked to begin unpaid.

faq.question: What happens when a method wins — who owns it?
faq.answer: It depends on the terms the host of a sealed test chose and published before anyone entered (Host a sealed test: /docs/host-a-sealed-test). There are three: the method becomes yours, passing to the people who hold the test; its maker keeps it, and you keep at most a locked copy for checking; or its maker keeps it but must publish it openly. For the first, Ownership & Terms (/docs/network/sovereignty/ownership-transfer) offers a Community Transfer Template: the method (code, weights, configuration, coaching data) goes to a governance body the community chooses, which owns it outright, while the developer keeps the right to publish the approach and permanent attribution. A place on the open leaderboard moves no rights. Champollion takes no share of any prize, or of anything a community earns from an asset it owns. No prize is open today, and no method has passed to a community under a contest's terms.

faq.question: How do I explore the languages Champollion knows, and fix something that's wrong?
faq.answer: Browse the Language Atlas at /languages: one card per language, with search and filters, where every value names the source it came from (The Atlas: /docs/atlas). Champollion is an index, not an arbiter: when sources disagree, as speaker counts often do, the card shows all of them, attributed, instead of picking one. A card says what a language is like and what resources exist for it; it never carries a translation score. If something is wrong, outdated or missing, every card has a "Suggest a correction or addition" link that opens the form with the language filled in (Submit to the Index: /docs/network/getting-started/submit-to-the-index). A maintainer reviews it and applies the cited fix at the source, so it sticks on the next build. If you'd rather your community's request not be public, write to info@champollion.dev.

faq.question: How should an AI agent use Champollion?
faq.answer: Point it at the agents' manual, For AI agents (/docs/agents), and have it read the operating contract first (/docs/agents/contract): what an agent may read, what it must ask the people, what it must never decide for them, and which rules the tools enforce. Then add the MCP server `champollion-mcp-server` (on npm). Its default profile is the rails: six tools (start_project, project_status, run_next_step, add_data, try_translation, explain) that walk one language project on the person's own computer. `--profile full` adds the rest: language cards, the benchmark queue, evaluations and training. {{UNRELEASED:The rails profile ships with the next release; the MCP server page (/docs/network/getting-started/mcp-server) says what the published version has.}} Every rails step is also an ordinary command (`champollion`, `nmt-forge`, `mt-eval`) for agents without MCP, and /llms.txt indexes the whole site.

faq.question: How do I contribute compute by running the benchmark queue?
faq.answer: The leaderboard has empty squares: language pair, method and condition combinations nobody has measured yet, kept in a public queue (Contributing Compute: /docs/network/getting-started/contributing-compute). Install the harness with `pipx install mt-eval-harness`, set one provider key (one OpenRouter key reaches every model in the queue), and run the highest-value open items with `mt-eval queue --top 5`. Add `--dry-run` first to see the plan and spend nothing. You don't need an account: results can publish as "anonymous", or sign in to put your name on the board, and either way they land as self-benchmarked. Queued datasets are openly licensed evaluation sets marked do-not-train; non-commercial and quarantined ones are left out. The Contribute page (/contribute) has the commands ready to copy.

faq.question: How do I raise an objection or request a takedown?
faq.answer: We genuinely want to hear it, in your own words, and you don't need an account (Your words, your rules: /docs/your-words-your-rules). Write to info@champollion.dev, or use this guide's message form (the chat panel → Send a message). To ask for something to be removed, put Takedown in the subject, or choose Takedown in the form. Our default is to act: we host almost no one's sentences, so most removals are a listing, a citation or a field on a page, and those we take down quickly. We say what we did, and if we can't do what you ask, we say why, and who decides. For a wrong fact on a language card, the card's "Suggest a correction or addition" link works too (The Atlas: /docs/atlas). Security problems go to security@champollion.dev.

faq.question: Can Champollion just translate something for me right now?
faq.answer: Not here: this site guide has no tools and can't translate anything. Champollion itself isn't an app you type into to get a translation today, either; it's the workshop where you build one (What this is: /docs/what-is-champollion). If you want a translator for your language, start with Before you begin (/docs/before-you-begin) and Start a project (/docs/start). {{UNRELEASED:The step-by-step tools come with the next version.}} If you have an app or a website, `npx champollion sync` translates its text with an AI model or a translation service you choose. Those send your text to the company that runs them, so use them for text that's fine to share (Translate an app or website: /docs/translate-an-app-or-website). For anything that matters, a fluent speaker has the last word.

faq.question: Can the site guide write code, debug, or run the harness for me?
faq.answer: No. This site guide is a tour of the docs, with no tools: it can't write code, debug, or run anything. The way to get that done is an AI assistant of your own, working on your computer: point it at the agents' manual (For AI agents: /docs/agents), which starts with the operating contract, at /llms.txt, and at the MCP server `champollion-mcp-server`. It can run the same commands a person would (Driving the rails from the shell: /docs/agents/shell), and it asks you whenever a decision is yours. Your assistant may have its own cost. If you'd like people beside you instead: "Having trouble, or want help with your project? Let's talk." (Getting help: /docs/getting-help).

faq.question: Will machine translation save or revitalize my language?
faq.answer: No, and we say so plainly. Translation Is Not Revitalization (/docs/network/perspectives/translation-is-not-revitalization) explains that machine translation converts text between languages, while revitalization creates new speakers. Those are different things, and no score changes that: children learn a language from people, not machines. What a translator can honestly do is bounded: give overloaded community translators a draft to review instead of translating from scratch, help with language-rights obligations, support adults learning the language, and become reusable tools, always under a fluent speaker's review, and only if a community decides it helps. A community deciding it doesn't help is a valid outcome, not a failure. As What it can't do yet (/docs/what-it-cant-do-yet) puts it, the language lives in its speakers, and in being used every day.

faq.question: Why is the project named 'Champollion'?
faq.answer: It's named for Jean-François Champollion, who deciphered Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822. He read the script through Coptic, the last stage of the Egyptian language, kept alive in the liturgy of the Coptic Church: the people who carry a language are the way in (On the name "Champollion": /docs/the-name). The page names the name's history plainly. Champollion worked inside a colonial enterprise, the Rosetta Stone reached Europe as military spoils, and "decipherment" can itself be an act of appropriation. What the project keeps is the method, not the man, and the tool is built to be the opposite of that extraction: collections aren't taken and kept, ownership stays with communities, and people are credited by name only where they have agreed. It's a non-Indigenous project, and a community that tells us the name does harm will be heard: info@champollion.dev.

faq.question: What datasets and language pairs can I benchmark against today?
faq.answer: Ask the tools: `mt-eval corpora --source eng --target <code>` lists the datasets that can run for a pair, with each one's size, contamination grade, domain and licence, and `--include-quarantined` adds the catalogued ones that can never run, each with its reason (Submission Rules: /docs/network/leaderboard/rules). Evaluation Datasets (/docs/network/leaderboard/datasets) describes the catalogue (open sets such as Tatoeba and Global Voices, the WMT sets, FLORES+ and more) and its licence lanes. No corpus content is hosted here: each dataset is a description pinned by its SHA-256 hash, and the harness fetches the reference sentences from their source at run time. A catalogue is what methods can be scored against, not a populated board. Three rules decide what can rank: a quarantined dataset never ranks (the EdTeKLA Plains Cree sets are catalogued as quarantined labels, and the database refuses any score posted against them); a set graded HIGH or MEDIUM for contamination, or not graded, is relative-only, so it compares methods but never reports absolute quality (FLORES+ is graded HIGH); and non-commercial sets stay out of every commercial and prize path.

faq.question: How is Champollion funded, who is behind it, and can I sponsor?
faq.answer: Champollion is a non-Indigenous project that works in a service role, and only by consent: a community decides what happens to its language, its data and anything built from it (Getting help: /docs/getting-help). Our docs don't set out how the project itself is funded. What they do say: Champollion takes no share of anything a community earns from its own language, and if a sponsor funds work, the money passes straight through (Who may use it, and what it costs: /docs/getting-started/who-may-use-this; Working with speakers: /docs/working-with-speakers). No prize is open today, and no prize money is held anywhere (Prize Specification: /docs/network/specifications/prizes). To talk about sponsoring a language's work, write to info@champollion.dev. And for your own project: "Having trouble, or want help with your project? Let's talk."
